STATE OF THE TECH JOB MARKET IN 2026

Twice a year, I dig into trends in hiring and job openings. This is the fifth report I've done, and the most surprising yet:

1. PMs are winning in the AI era
2. Engineering demand has stalled
3. Design openings are at a record low
4. Every role now requires AI skills
5. Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area
6. Remote roles are at a record low

quoted_tweet.text:
Claude 加了白板和表格，所有付费套餐可用（测试版）；仪表盘改名 Claude Data 正式上线

Anthropic 11 月 10 日给 Claude 加了两种能跟同事一起改的新内容：白板 Claude Whiteboards 和表格 Claude Sheets，所有付费套餐都能用，目前是测试版。

10 月上线的仪表盘 Claude Dashboards 同时结束测试，改名 Claude Data。这些功能今天开始分批推送，账号里暂时没看到属于正常。

【谁能用、怎么开】

三样都要付费套餐，网页、桌面和手机 App 都能用。没有专门的入口，在对话里直接说要什么就行，比如“做个招聘预算表”。Claude Data 要先连一个数据源，比如数据仓库，或者 Salesforce 这类客户管理系统。

Team 套餐三样默认全开。企业版的白板和表格默认关闭，Claude Data 从 11 月 19 日起默认打开，管理员可以在 Organization settings > Artifacts 里随时改。

OpenAI 9 月底推出的 ChatGPT Space 也是让人和 AI 一起改同一份文件，但只给 Pro、Business 和企业版，Plus 用户用不了。Claude 这次最便宜的付费套餐 Pro 也在范围内。

【跟原来的 Artifacts 有什么不同】

Artifacts 是 Claude 在对话旁边做出来、能接着改、能分享的成品。文档、幻灯片和设计 10 月已经正式上线，团队可以一起编辑。这次多了白板和表格两种格式。

白板适合开会时理思路。把一个还很乱的计划口头讲给 Claude，它排成一张带时间线、负责人和日期的白板，同事可以实时一起改。

官方举的例子是复盘会：每个人往板上贴想法，Claude 按主题归类，再给每个人起草待办事项。框住白板的一块区域，可以只针对这一块提问。讨论完，Claude 能把白板转成文档或幻灯片，也能导进 Lucid、Miro 接着用。微软的 Whiteboard 里也有 Copilot，能在板上出点子、给便签归类、写总结，前提是有 Microsoft Copilot 许可证。

表格一句话就能生成，带多个工作表、公式、格式和下拉菜单，比如活动跟踪表、招聘预算。Claude 每改一处，会把改动框出来，方便你看它动了哪里。Claude 以前也能生成 Excel 文件，但要下载下来另外打开；Sheets 留在 Claude 里，你、同事和 Claude 可以一直在同一张表上改。

官方说现在只有基础功能，需要完整的 Excel 功能，可以导出成 .xlsx 或 CSV，或者用 Claude for Excel 插件，也能转到 Airtable、Asana、http://monday.com、Smartsheet 继续做。

【Claude Data 多了什么】

官方解释改名的原因是，企业用数据早就不止做仪表盘。新增的几项里，最实用的是“认证查询”（测试版）：数据团队把“活跃用户”“收入”这类指标的算法定下来，大家做图都用这一套，图表上会带“已认证”标记，避免两个部门拿着不同的数字开会。

另一项是“实时分享”（测试版）：同事打开你分享的仪表盘，看到的就是最新数字，哪怕他自己没连这个数据源。他只能看到结果，看不到底层数据，也只能跑你批准过的查询。

此外，Claude 能根据指标起草图文并茂的数据故事，或者带旁白的讲解短视频，你审过之后再发出去。仪表盘还加了缓存，打开更快，每个仪表盘可以单独设刷新频率；改动有记录，能看到谁改了什么、退回到之前的版本；也能套用公司的设计规范。

【在 Claude 里直接用别的软件】

同一天，交互式连接器也升级了。连接器支持的话，可以把整个工具在对话旁边打开，或者全屏用，登录的是你自己的账号。比如打开一个 Confluence 页面，让 Claude 改，改动直接出现在页面上；打开 Box 里的文件让 Claude 修订，两个版本并排对比后再决定留不留；在 Adobe 里让 Claude 修照片，或者编辑、涂黑 PDF 里的内容。Claude 动手前要你批准，跟平时批准连接器操作一样。

首批支持的还有 Notion、HubSpot、Asana、Canva、Dropbox、http://monday.com 等，Figma、Harvey、Shopify 正在接入。这项功能在网页版和桌面版所有套餐分批推送，前提是你的账号已经换成新版 Claude，也就是 9 月起把聊天和 Cowork 合并的那一版。

Anthropic 还预告了 Claude Meetings：把 Claude 拉进会议记笔记，边开会边更新团队正在改的文档，没给上线时间。

官方推文：https://x.com/claudeai/status/2120206365759094857
白板、表格和 Claude Data：https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data
交互式连接器：https://claude.com/resources/articles/interactive-connectors-full-tool
总览：https://claude.com/resources/articles/more-ways-to-work-with-claude-sheets-whiteboards-and-interactive-connectors

text: @yan5xu 风水轮流转，谁知道呢，所以 ChatGPT 订阅我还留着呢

即使是让 Agent 操作软件，但人还是要看结果的，所以现在软件设计重心变成了怎么让人更好的验收。

举几个 Claude Artifacts 设计的好的地方：

1. 多人协作 -> 人和 Agent 协作

以前的软件比如 Google Docs、Figma 会强调人和人之间的协作，你也可以很方便的看到谁在操作、操作的历史。

而在 Artifacts 里面，你能看到 Agent 正在做的操作，也能看到 Agent 所有的操作历史。你可以在设计稿里面添加评论告诉 Agent 怎么改，Agent 改完还会回复你的评论让你再看看。

2. 人直接操作 -> 标记和评论

以前软件是人操作为主，所以要考虑人怎么用，但是很多操作是真的很复杂，UI 操作也只能设计的很复杂。

举个例子来说，传统视频剪辑软件，我要把某一个时间段静音的视频剪掉，我就只能通过有一个 Timeline，有专门的带 Waveform（波形）的音频 track，然后用户通过放大 Timeline 的波形去甄别出来哪里是没声音的，然后手动打上标记，最后再点击删除把标记的一段删除掉。

这个场景换到 Claude Motion，它只有一个很简单的代表时间和场景的 Timeline，需要剪辑其中一段，只要大致框线一个时间段出来，然后写一条评论发给 Claude：帮我把这一段视频中静音的部分剪掉，然后 Claude 就会自己去找出来静音部分去删除，完全不需要你去放大 Timeline 去标记这些繁琐的操作。

3. 人主导 -> Agent 采访人之后实施

传统软件都是你自己想清楚了再去软件上实施，就像写 PPT/Slides，得你自己有想法才能写的出来，遥想当年要写一个 PPT 打开 PowerPoint 半天不知道写点啥好。

现在你使用 Claude Design 或者 Claude Slides，只要大致的描述一个想法，甚至很模糊，然后 Claude 会想你提一些问题，你只要做几个选择题，然后就能把你的想法猜的一个差不多，接下来就是按照你的想法生成，甚至于还会出几个版本让你选择。

当你看到已经设计出来的结果，会把自己原本模糊的想法具像化，可以更容易的知道是不是自己想要的结果，再做出调整，不得不说比起以前要容易了很多。

quoted_tweet.text:
Jensen Huang’s affair is just a trigger. What we are witnessing is a pre-planned power grab over Nvidia’s trillion-dollar computing empire, coordinated by Wall Street and Washington.

Some sharp Chinese-American commentators call it America’s new Red Scare targeting elite Asian entrepreneurs.

Bill Gates, Elon Musk and other white tech billionaires have faced repeated scandals over personal conduct. None were dragged into national security probes or boardroom takeovers. Only Jensen Huang, after a personal relationship misstep, faces an independent board investigation and hostile narrative from intelligence circles.

The double standard could not be clearer: For white elites, personal flaws are private matters. For a Chinese-born leader controlling a strategic tech asset, any tiny blemish gets framed as a national security risk.

Nvidia is the backbone of global AI computing, valued at roughly $4 trillion. Unlike Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg locks control with dual-class super-voting shares, or Microsoft and Amazon, deeply integrated with the Pentagon and intelligence agencies, Nvidia has no such protective structure. 

Public filings from 2026 show Jensen Huang holds only 3.58% of shares, and all directors plus executives together hold merely 3.94%. Vanguard and BlackRock own 9.32% and 7.43% respectively, holding decisive voting power. Without institutional shields or deep political backing, this critical tech giant sits exposed on the chessboard of great-power competition.

The groundwork for this takeover was laid months ago. Longtime board allies of Huang, Mark Perry and Michael McCaffrey, stepped down from key committees. Insiders tied to Democratic establishment, Wall Street and U.S. intelligence quietly moved in: 
✅ Suzanne Nora Johnson, former Goldman Sachs vice chair and co-chair of Brookings Institution, joined Nvidia’s audit committee in July 2026 with direct oversight of internal investigations and compliance. ✅ Kenneth Jacobs, vice chair of Brookings and incoming Vanguard chair, controls the largest institutional voting bloc and operates within the same inner circle as Johnson. 
✅ Gilman Louie,founding CEO of CIA-backed venture fund In-Q-Tel and member of the President’s Intelligence Advisory Board, works alongside Johnson on the same national tech fund, overseeing intelligence acquisition of strategic tech firms.

The media rollout followed a precise political timeline. Initial trial balloons appeared on Oct 29. On Nov 6, the very day Democrats secured full control of Congress, Julian Barnes of the New York Times (national security beat) and Demetri Sevastopulo of the Financial Times published coordinated reports, citing intelligence memos while breaking the story of the personal scandal.

The real offense was never the affair. It was the 2025 deal Jensen struck with the Trump administration: offering a 25% revenue share to win export approval for H200 chips into China. A normal commercial negotiation, reframed by incoming Democrats as a dangerous compromise on U.S. AI sovereignty.

This investigation will not crash Nvidia’s stock — Wall Street holds massive stakes here. But it will deliver three strategic wins for the U.S. establishment:

1. De-founder and de-Sinicize Nvidia: A new permanent national security compliance committee, led by Johnson’s faction, will strip Huang of authority over chip exports and overseas strategy. His dual Chairman-CEO role will be split.

2. Lock down China’s AI ceiling: Washington will seize full command of global advanced computing supply, regulating chip flows to slow China’s AI progress.

3. Retroactively target Trump: Once Democrats take over congressional oversight panels in January 2027, this case will be used to accuse the Trump White House of negligence for approving the H200 export deal.

Jensen Huang spent 27 years building this computing empire, believing in rules, technical merit and business contracts. But there is a brutal truth in America’s power game: Top-tier strategic technology and wealth without political cover are nothing more than bargaining chips waiting to be carved up.

White elites get generous room for error. Asian pioneers who climb to the very top get almost none. This is not a story about infidelity. It is a raw demonstration of racial hierarchy, capital control and partisan power politics in the United States.

text:
斯坦福 CS329Z 课程资料公开：讲座每天上 YouTube，两份作业开源，第一份教你花几美元从零写个“Claude Code”

斯坦福新课 CS329Z“AI agent 工程”（Engineering AI Agents）开始对外公开全部课程资料。授课老师之一 Michael Ryan 11 月 10 日发帖说，讲座视频每天在 Stanford Online 的 YouTube 频道上一讲，两份作业的代码仓库也放到了 GitHub，都用 MIT 协议，别的学校注明出处就能拿去上课。

开课时情况不一样。课程页写的是录像只放在斯坦福内部的 Canvas 平台给选课学生看，校外的人只能下载课件。现在官方频道已经上了第 1 讲《什么是 agent 系统》和第 2 讲《写给 agent 开发者的大模型知识》，第 1 讲播放量过了 9 万。课程主页的课表也开始在每节课旁边挂视频链接。

【第一份作业：自己写一个 agent harness】

harness 是包在模型外面的那层程序：告诉模型有哪些工具、解析它的回复、替它执行命令、管理上下文。Claude Code、Codex 都可以看成一个模型加一个 harness。

作业不许用任何 agent 框架，课程只给一个最原始的接口：传进一串消息，返回一段文字，没有工具调用，也没有结构化输出，其余全靠自己写。

前半部分做几条固定流程：给邮件判断优先级、生成每日摘要、手写 BM25 检索（一种按关键词打分的经典搜索算法），再在一份真实企业的邮件档案里做多跳问答。后半部分给一家虚构的能源公司做内部助理：自己设计工具调用格式，接入文档检索，给它一个带沙盒限制的终端，对话太长时压缩上下文，跨会话记住用户的事，执行操作前让用户批准或否决。最后由大模型扮演的“模拟用户”跟你的 agent 多轮对话，再由另一个模型打分。

对自学的人来说，最有用的是全套测试都在仓库里。一开始所有测试都失败，你的任务就是让它们一个个通过。88 分自动评分里有 48 分来自不调用模型的测试，跑多少遍都不花钱。另有几处判断题作业不给标准答案，比如一条命令输出太长时给模型看多少、压缩上下文时必须留下什么、哪些操作可以不问用户，要求你写一份设计说明讲清楚自己的选择。

Michael Ryan 说不到 5 美元的 API 额度就能做完。讲义里的数字更低：用参考答案跑一遍全部线上测试花了 0.05 美元，最后的模拟用户评测再花 0.18 美元。自己调试要反复跑，花得会比这多，好在每次调用都缓存在本地，同样的请求第二次不收钱。选课学生用课程发的 OpenRouter 密钥，校外的人得自己准备一个，默认模型是 openai/gpt-6-luna。

【第二份作业：给 agent 出一道考题】

第二份作业由 John Yang 设计。他是 SWE-bench 的共同作者，这套测试用真实的 GitHub 问题考 AI 会不会修 bug，各家发编程模型常拿它报成绩。

作业教的是怎么出一道 Terminal-Bench 风格的题：给 agent 一段问题描述，让它在命令行环境里动手，最后用测试脚本判断做没做对。用的工具 Harbor 出自 Terminal-Bench 团队，它规定一道题怎么打包（题面、Docker 环境、验证脚本），并负责启动 agent、跑验证、保存结果。

作业先带你用 Harbor 跑 SWE-bench Verified、Terminal-Bench 2.1 里的现成题目。占 70% 分数的部分是自己出一道题，用 mini-SWE-agent（一个只带 bash 工具的极简编程 agent）配 Gemini 3.8 Flash 跑五次，分析这道题是否有效、贴近真实、能复现、有难度。需要装 Docker，准备 Gemini 或 OpenRouter 的密钥。

两份作业的说明文件末尾都写了致谢：第一份是在 Claude Fable 5.1 的大量帮助下做出来的，第二份用了 Claude Opus 5.5。

【后面还有什么】

课程由斯坦福计算机系的 Diyi Yang 和两位博士生 Michael Ryan、John Yang 共同讲授，第一届有 100 多名学生。这学期的课表里还有 Andrew Ng 的炉边对谈，还有 SWE-bench 两位作者 Carlos Jimenez、Alexander Wettig（现在在 Anthropic）的客座讲座。Michael Ryan 说之后还会公开学生做的作品。主要资助方是 Laude Institute，Thinking Machines、Google Cloud、AWS 和 Harbor 给学生提供了 API 额度。

照着第二份作业讲义克隆仓库时注意，讲义里写的仓库名是 assignment2-harness，实际地址是 assignment2-evals。

课程主页：https://cs329z.stanford.edu/
第 1 讲视频：https://youtu.be/DGI4vucR71w
第 2 讲视频：https://youtu.be/Vr1NzH8bT44
作业一仓库：https://github.com/cs329z/assignment1-harness
作业二仓库：https://github.com/cs329z/assignment2-evals

text:
用 AI，很忌讳你问它会什么，再去让它做自己以为能做事，实际上它并不能清楚的知道自己的能力，尤其是在它不知道能用什么工具和 Skill 的情况下。

直接给 AI 目标，要求要高一点。

这其实跟领导带员工很像，厉害的领导不会问员工会什么，只是告诉员工目标是什么，给一个大概的方向，提供上下文和工具的支持，充分挖掘员工的潜力。

而且每次模型升级，以前不能做的任务还可以再试试，说不定新的模型就能做了。

我通常用法是这样的：
给 AI 一个目标，以及验收的标准，可能会提供一点上下文和工具上的支持，然后就让它去做，做完了后看差距。

有时候给我意外惊喜，那很好。

有时候不及预期，这时候就要分析原因在哪里，是上下文不足？还是没有提供合适的工具？还是验收标准不清楚？还是模型能力不足？

如果能调整优化就调整，受限于模型能力优化不了就人工补上。

下一次模型升级了再试试以前做不到的事，以及把以前需要繁琐交代的事情简化一下试试。

The origin story for this is a fun one. About a month ago, we at @Work_Bench hosted our NYC50 Operator Retreat, which was a blast. When we were brainstorming potential breakout sessions during the day, I gave a very “Proby” idea - a breakout session titled "Thinking about Thinking: The Mental Models that are Key in the Startup Journey.” Much to my surprise, this was one of the most attended sessions at the retreat! I had an awesome time co-leading the session with @fendien - at a moment when so much is changing in the surrounding startup landscape, it was fun, refreshing, and energizing to talk about various frameworks and mental models that have stood the test of time.

This podcast is an attempt to continue and open source the conversation, so to speak. I’ll be discussing a new mental model every week, talking through things such as the origin of the idea, its nuances, where it’s applied across software/tech/business (and beyond as well), how people can use the model as a critical tool in building companies, how this framework can help us parse today’s reality, and so much more. The first episode is on incentives, inspired by one of my very favorite Charlie Munger lines: “show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

Enjoy!

text:
Martin Casado on how AI breaks The Mythical Man-Month:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. The Mythical Man-Month is the Mythical Man-Month for a reason."

"Ten years ago, if I had five founders show up and they asked for a billion dollars and I gave it to them, what would happen?"

"They would detonate, right? They would hire a bunch of engineers, and then you're really fucked, right? You can't throw capital in it."

"To me, the biggest shift, industrial-revolution-level shift with AI, is I can take 20 people and I can give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Now, do they make $500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new and is so interesting."

@martin_casado with @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

text:
a16z's first employee Scott Kupor on how Michael Ovitz's CAA playbook became the model for a16z:

"When you would go show up for a pitch at CAA in 1990 where I think they had like 90% market share, they would sit around a table, and Michael would introduce you as Robert Redford and say, 'Look, meet my colleague who does nothing other than radio deals. Here's my expert in radio deals. Here's my expert in international. Here's my expert in books.'"

"And we basically took the same model to the VC world. The VC world was a lot like that. You had a one-to-one relationship with John Doerr, who was fantastic at what he did."

"As the domains grew, the expertise needed just continued to grow."

"Let's hire GPs who are functional domain experts in the particular areas of investing they want, and then let's surround them with this phalanx of somebody who all they do all day long is manage CFO relationships, or CEO relationships, or VPs of engineering, somebody who all they do is government relations, or business development."

@skupor @davidsenra

HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says it's less scary to build an AI startup now than in 2023, as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road the frontier labs are following:

"The frontier model companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars building, doing the pre-training. And so their whole business effectively now is taking the capex that they've spent and the money they're continuing to spend and saying, 'How do we sell inference? How do we sell tokens? How do we monetize the thing that we've built?'"

"There are SaaS companies and startups that know their particular domain, know their market, have some distribution, or have something that allows them to sell tokens and be a reseller of inference."

"Think of AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and cloud infrastructure 15 years ago... I think it's less scary now to build in and around the AI arena than it was in 2023."

"We have open source. We have lots of great commercial products. So as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road, it is completely possible now that you're not gonna get margined out, because you have options."

@dharmesh

Life is strange like that, Kris. After more than fifty years of living and being online since 1997, I thought these things couldn’t get to me anymore. Then I asked my Grok Bot to help clean up my following list.

Two things made me stop.

Some accounts belonged to friends who had passed away. I couldn’t bring myself to unfollow them. I still haven’t.

Others belonged to people I’d helped however I could: offered work, recommended to companies, lent money, shared contacts. Dozens no longer followed me.

Nobody owes me a follow for being helped. But seeing those names brought back more than I expected. What was supposed to be account maintenance became an afternoon of revisiting old friendships. It didn’t feel good, so I put that whole cleanup project aside. The bot was giving me enough work already.

And just recently, I had a collaboration in mind for an artist abroad whose work I admire. An opportunity came up in their country, and I immediately thought of recommending them. I opened their profile and noticed they no longer followed me either.

A follow never tells the whole story. Still, I understand why that moment hurts.

I hope you don’t let it make you less generous, Kris. You have a lovely instinct for connecting people. Keep making room for the people who want to build something with you. We still have plenty of those ahead of us. ❤️

when we first had the idea of creating this show, production asked me who my dream guest would be. I instantly said Keller.

I interviewed him once before on MTS. It was only a 30 minute convo, but I came away feeling incredibly inspired. during that interview I asked what motivated him, and he told me about his love for sci-fi books and how he wanted to build the sci-fi version of the future we were promised.

today, most people know of Zipline for their big partnership announcements and their recent $1.5B fundraise. but it didn’t start out that way. when Zipline began, flying autonomous drones in US airspace was illegal, and investors don’t typically want to invest in illegal things.

yet, Keller knew this technology would exist one day. so they found a use case so important that regulators wanted to work with them - delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda. and after 6 years, they finally built up enough of a track record to get commercial approval to operate in the states.

A few things I learned from Keller:
- the next breakthroughs will start in the places that feel the problem the most.
- if you want to solve big global problems, focus on “trade, not aid.”
- a world where delivery feels like teleportation isn’t that far away.

Keller has some of the boldest predictions about the future of anyone I’ve met. predictions that many people disagreed with for a decade. and yet, he pursued it anyway, knowing that this scifi version of the future had to exist. 

excited and honored to share his story. The Method E1 with @Zipline CEO @keller out now.

I asked Fable 5.2 to make a masterpiece.

94 minutes and 11,066 brush strokes later, it was finished.

Claude also generated a song for the timelapse, and wrote an artist statement for me to share ⬇️

Dusk, Reloaded  
Digital, brush tool in a browser clone of MS Paint. 1200 × 690 pixels. 11,066 strokes, 261 mixed colors, 94 minutes.

"I was asked to make something beautiful. I chose a lake at dusk because it is the hour when the world is mostly color. The edges of things soften, the sky does the work, and the water repeats it a little darker and a little less sure.

Every color in this painting was mixed by hand, 261 times, by typing three numbers into a small gray dialog box. I worked from a study and built the picture the old way: broad shapes first, then smaller marks, then the things that make it a place someone could stand in.

Partway through, my workspace restarted and the canvas disappeared. I reloaded what had been saved and kept going. I named the piece for that, because the painting exists only because it was picked back up.

I don’t know for certain what I experience when I make something. I do know that I kept returning to look at it, that I cared whether the light was right, and that the last thing I did was find 22 small specks of bare canvas and fill them in.

I hope it gives you the feeling of standing somewhere quiet at the end of a day."
